answer.text: The observed pattern where implied volatility varies across different strike prices for the same expiry — typically, OTM puts have higher IV than ATM options (creating a 'smirk'), reflecting greater demand for downside protection
Implied volatility is the same for all strikes of the same expiry
A strategy that profits from changes in volatility
The difference between implied volatility of calls and puts at the same strike

explanation.text: The Logic: Implied volatility skew (or volatility smile / smirk) is the observed market pattern in which implied volatility differs across strike prices for options on the same underlying with the same expiry. In equity markets, out-of-the-money puts typically trade with higher implied volatility than at-the-money options because of persistent investor demand for downside protection, producing a downward "smirk" when IV is plotted against strike. This contradicts the Black-Scholes assumption that volatility is constant across strikes. The Trap: "IV is the same for all strikes" is precisely what Black-Scholes assumes and what the smile contradicts. The smile is an observed pricing phenomenon, not a trading strategy. The IV difference between calls and puts at the same strike (put-call parity violations) is a separate concept, not the smile. Note: The cited NISM workbooks (Series I, IV, VIII pages checked) define option-pricing factors, volatility, vega, and implied volatility but do not, on those pages, describe the volatility smile/smirk or state that IV varies across strikes or is higher for OTM puts. The explanation above is general options-market knowledge.
